summary: RPL is an IPv6 routing protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks, where routers have little processing power, memory, and battery, and links are lossy and unstable. It is a distance vector protocol that builds a directed acyclic graph and supports several traffic patterns.

plainLanguage.summary: RPL is a routing protocol for networks of small, battery-powered devices, such as sensors, that talk over weak radio links. It builds a tree-like structure toward one central point, so devices can send data even when links appear and disappear. The protocol became a Proposed Standard in 2012 and is still the basis for IPv6 routing in these networks.

subtitle: How tiny, battery-powered devices on flaky radio links build routes to a central point and back.

tldr.problem: Low-power and lossy networks have routers with little processing power, memory and battery, linked by unstable low-rate links, and their traffic mostly flows to or from a central control point rather than between arbitrary pairs.
tldr.mechanism: RPL organizes the network as a destination-oriented directed acyclic graph (DODAG) rooted at a sink. Nodes learn parents from DIO messages, rank themselves below those parents to avoid loops, and optionally send DAO messages upward to build downward routes.
tldr.outcome: RPL is a Proposed Standard that leaves the optimization goal to pluggable Objective Functions, and it has since been updated by RFC 9008, RFC 9010, RFC 9685, RFC 9914 and RFC 9926.

facts.label: Global / local instances
facts.value: up to 128 global, 64 local per DODAGID

today: RFC 6550 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 9008, RFC 9010, RFC 9685, RFC 9914 and RFC 9926, so check those for changes to its behavior. The Objective Functions, metrics, data-plane option and source-routing header that it relies on are specified in companion documents such as RFC 6551, RFC 6552, RFC 6553 and RFC 6554.

sections.title: The Problem Low-Power Networks Face
sections.content:
Low-power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) are made of constrained nodes: little processing power, little memory, and sometimes little energy. Their links carry low data rates, lose packets often, and change over time. A network can hold up to thousands of nodes. The traffic pattern matters as much as the size: most packets go from many nodes toward one point, from one point to many nodes, or between pairs that communicate rarely. The RFC was written to meet application requirements collected in RFC 5867, RFC 5826, RFC 5673 and RFC 5548, but it is not limited to those applications.

Five principles shape the design. A network may run several RPL Instances at once, each serving a different goal. RPL separates packet forwarding from the routing decision: companion documents define Objective Functions that turn measurements such as energy or latency into route choices. Links must work in both directions before a neighbor is used, so a node verifies reachability, for example with Neighbor Unreachability Detection. RPL depends on no particular link layer. And because radio traffic costs energy, the protocol uses the Trickle algorithm of RFC 6206 to keep control messages rare once the network is stable.
sections.plainLanguage: Sensors run on small batteries and talk over unreliable radio. RPL moves their data with very few control messages, because every transmission costs power.

sections.title: Instances, DODAGs and Versions
sections.content:
RPL shapes a network into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) split into one or more Destination Oriented DAGs (DODAGs), one per sink. The sink is the DODAG root. Four values identify and maintain the topology: the RPLInstanceID, the DODAGID, the DODAGVersionNumber and the Rank. All DODAGs in one RPL Instance share the same Objective Function, and the pair (RPLInstanceID, DODAGID) names a single DODAG.

A DODAG root repairs the whole topology at once by incrementing the DODAGVersionNumber, which starts a new DODAG Version. In the new Version, nodes may choose a position whose Rank is not constrained by their Rank in the old one. RPL also allows repair inside a Version, with limits the root sets.

An Instance is either global or local. A global RPLInstanceID is coordinated across the network, and the RFC allows up to 128 global instances. A local RPLInstanceID is allocated by the single root that owns the DODAGID, with up to 64 local instances per DODAGID. A DODAG is grounded when its root can meet the goal the application set, and floating otherwise; floating DODAGs can still carry traffic inside the network during repair.

RPL carries three traffic patterns: many nodes toward a root, from a root to many nodes, and node-to-node, where a packet climbs toward the root until it reaches an ancestor that knows a route down to the destination.
sections.plainLanguage: The network forms a tree-like graph with the sink at the top. Every message states which instance and which version of the graph it belongs to, so nodes that disagree about the topology do not mix their data.

sections.title: Rank and Loop Avoidance
sections.content:
Rank states where a node sits in a DODAG Version. It strictly increases going down, away from the root, and strictly decreases going up. Rank is not a path cost and has no physical unit: the Objective Function decides how it is computed from metrics. Rank is compared as DAGRank(rank) = floor(rank/MinHopRankIncrease). The rule that prevents loops is simple: the Rank a node advertises MUST be greater than the Rank of every one of its parents.

RPL also forbids greediness. A node that tried to move deeper to collect extra parents, while listening to advertisements from nodes deeper than itself, could start a feedback loop in which nodes keep rejoining deeper and deeper. So a node stays at a Rank that fits its most preferred parent and ignores advertisements from deeper nodes, except in some forms of local repair. A node may not advertise a Rank higher than the lowest it has advertised plus DAGMaxRankIncrease in the same Version; beyond that it advertises INFINITE_RANK (0xFFFF), which also withdraws its routes.

The RFC is direct about the limits: RPL guarantees neither loop-free path selection nor fast convergence. Instead it detects and repairs a loop when a packet uses one, with Rank information carried in the packets themselves. A lost advertisement can create a DODAG loop, and a lost No-Path DAO can create a route loop at the root.
sections.plainLanguage: Every node gets a number that must be larger than the numbers of its parents. Because the numbers only grow away from the root, a packet following them cannot travel in a circle.

sections.title: The ICMPv6 Control Messages
sections.content:
RPL control messages are a new ICMPv6 message with Type 155. The Code field names the message: 0x00 DODAG Information Solicitation (DIS), 0x01 DODAG Information Object (DIO), 0x02 Destination Advertisement Object (DAO), 0x03 DAO acknowledgement (DAO-ACK) and 0x8A Consistency Check. The high bit of the Code (0x80) marks a secured variant, giving 0x80 to 0x83 for the secured forms of the first four. A message with an unknown Code MUST be dropped without a response.

Most control messages stay on one link: the source is a link-local address and the destination is either the all-RPL-nodes multicast address ff02::1a or a link-local unicast address. The exception is DAO and DAO-ACK in Non-Storing mode, which cross multiple hops between global or unique-local addresses.

The DIS asks neighbors whether any DODAG is nearby. The DIO carries what a node needs to discover an Instance, learn its configuration, choose parents and maintain the DODAG: the RPLInstanceID, Version Number, the sender's Rank, the Grounded flag, the Mode of Operation, the DODAGPreference, the DTSN and the DODAGID. The DAO carries destination information upward with a DAOSequence and the flags K (please acknowledge) and D (DODAGID present). A DAO-ACK echoes the DAOSequence with a Status, where 0 means unqualified acceptance. The Consistency Check message resynchronizes security counters and runs challenge-responses between neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: RPL uses one special ICMPv6 packet type for all of its control messages. The code inside says what the message does, from asking whether a DODAG exists to announcing a destination.

sections.title: Control Message Options
sections.content:
Options follow the base object in a type-length-value format, where the length counts octets. (Neighbor Discovery options count units of 8 octets instead; RPL does not.) A receiver MUST silently ignore an option type it does not recognize and continue with the next one.

The options defined here are 0x00 Pad1, 0x01 PadN, 0x02 DAG Metric Container (metrics defined in RFC 6551), 0x03 Route Information, 0x04 DODAG Configuration, 0x05 RPL Target, 0x06 Transit Information, 0x07 Solicited Information, 0x08 Prefix Information and 0x09 RPL Target Descriptor.

The DODAG Configuration option is set by the root and must not be changed by other nodes. It carries the Trickle parameters, MaxRankIncrease, MinHopRankIncrease, the Objective Code Point, the default route lifetime and its unit, the Path Control Size, and an A flag that turns on authenticated security mode. Route Information and Prefix Information reuse the Neighbor Discovery options from RFC 4191 and RFC 4861, so a node can form an address from a prefix its parent offers. In a Prefix Information option the R flag means the prefix field holds the sender's full address, which children can use as the parent address in their Transit Information.

An RPL Target names an address, a prefix or a multicast group that is reachable along the DODAG. Transit Information describes the path to it: a Path Sequence, a Path Lifetime and, in Non-Storing mode, the parent address. A Path Lifetime of zero means the destination is no longer reachable, and a DAO that says so is called a No-Path. Solicited Information lets a DIS filter who answers, by matching the version, the instance or the DODAGID.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages can carry extra options, each with a type and a length. One option holds the whole DODAG's configuration; others announce addresses and the paths to them. Unknown option types are ignored.

sections.title: Building and Maintaining Upward Routes
sections.content:
Nodes advertise themselves by multicasting DIOs on the link. Every non-root node picks a parent set from its candidate neighbors, and one of those parents is the preferred parent used for the default upward route. A root has an empty parent set, and every parent must have a lower Rank than the node itself. A non-root node MUST advertise the same Grounded flag, Mode of Operation, DODAGPreference, Version, RPLInstanceID and DODAGID as its preferred parent, so those values pass down the graph unchanged, while Rank and DTSN change at every hop. When Neighbor Unreachability Detection or an equivalent check finds a neighbor unreachable, routes through it MUST be removed. RPL defines no keepalives of its own: periodic keepalives would cost too much bandwidth and energy in these networks.

DIOs are sent on a Trickle timer (RFC 6206), so a stable network sends them rarely and a changing one sends them often. A node resets the timer when it finds a forwarding inconsistency, hears a multicast DIS it should answer, or joins a new DODAG Version. A unicast DIS is answered with a unicast DIO that includes the DODAG Configuration option.

A node joins by letting its Objective Function choose parents from metrics and constraints. It should confirm that the link is bidirectional and good enough before using a candidate. To limit erratic movement, a node SHOULD keep its previous parent choice when metrics are equal, and SHOULD filter out parents whose availability fluctuates when steadier choices exist. A node that cannot follow the Instance's Objective Function or metrics, or that wants to save energy, can join as a leaf: it advertises INFINITE_RANK and does not extend the DODAG. A node that loses all parents may detach and become the root of its own floating DODAG.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node advertises its rank and picks parents that are closer to the root. It advertises often while the network changes and rarely once everything has settled.

sections.title: Downward Routes: Storing and Non-Storing
sections.content:
Downward routes are optional. The root's Mode of Operation (MOP) in the DIO says which kind a DODAG offers, and a node that cannot honor it can only join as a leaf. MOP 0 means no Downward routes, 1 Non-Storing, 2 Storing without multicast and 3 Storing with multicast. With MOP 0, nodes MUST NOT send DAOs. No implementation is expected to support both Storing and Non-Storing, and mixed-mode operation is not supported.

Nodes send DAOs upward to their DAO parents, a subset of their DODAG parents. In Non-Storing mode every DAO travels directly to the root, listing the sender's parents in Transit Information options. The root assembles each full path, and downward packets carry a source-routing header (RFC 6554), so intermediate nodes keep no downward tables. In Storing mode DAOs move one hop at a time to link-local parents, every non-root, non-leaf node stores routes for its own sub-DODAG, and downward packets are routed by destination address.

A DAO sender can set the K flag to request a DAO-ACK. A node delays its own DAO with a timer (DelayDAO, default 1 second) so it can combine information from several children before sending one message. A parent can request fresh DAOs from its sub-DODAG by increasing its DTSN. The Path Control field in Transit Information lets a node spread a destination's routes among its DAO parents, with four two-bit preference subfields, PC1 the most preferred; the default Path Control Size of 0 limits a node to a single parent. A node that drops a DAO parent SHOULD send a No-Path DAO in Storing mode so the stale route is removed. A node may also multicast a DAO to ff02::1a, but only to advertise its own information to one-hop neighbors, which allows direct peer-to-peer traffic without the DODAG relaying it.
sections.plainLanguage: Upward routing needs only a list of parents. Downward routing is optional: either each node stores routes for the devices below it, or the root keeps the full paths and writes them onto each packet.

sections.title: Forwarding and Loop Detection in Data Packets
sections.content:
RPL detects loops when a data packet is forwarded, not when the topology changes. Packets carry RPL Packet Information in an external carrier such as the IPv6 option of RFC 6553. It holds a Down flag O, a Rank-Error flag R, a Forwarding-Error flag F, the RPLInstanceID and a 16-bit SenderRank. This information is required on every packet except those source-routed down in Non-Storing mode, which cannot loop.

A receiver finds an inconsistency when a packet marked Down arrives from a node of higher Rank, or a packet marked Up arrives from a node of lower Rank. The node tolerates one error: it sets the Rank-Error bit and forwards. A second detection on the same packet means the packet MUST be dropped and the Trickle timer MUST be reset, which spreads the word that the DODAG needs repair.

The RFC also gives non-normative advice on picking a next hop, in order: source route, multicast-learned routes, unicast Downward routes by Path Control preference, DODAG parents, and otherwise drop. A successor MUST NOT be the same node as the predecessor, except when a packet turns from Up to Down. In Storing mode, a node that finds its Downward route stale can return the packet toward the parent with the Forwarding-Error bit set, so the stale state is cleaned up along the sub-DODAG. In Non-Storing mode the root gets an ICMPv6 'Error in Source Routing Header' message (Destination Unreachable, code 7) instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Every data packet can carry the direction it should travel and the rank of its sender. When those two facts disagree twice in a row, the node drops the packet and tells the network to repair its routes.

sections.title: Security Modes and Threats
sections.content:
Security is OPTIONAL to implement, because many LLN devices cannot afford the cost and many deployments rely on link-layer protection instead. An implementation may support any subset. The RFC describes three modes: unsecured, with plain messages; preinstalled, where a node holding a preinstalled key can join as host or router; and authenticated, where a preinstalled key allows joining only as a host, and a second key from a key authority is required to become a router. Keys are provided by higher-layer processes; how to obtain them is left to future specifications.

A secured message carries a Security section between the ICMPv6 checksum and the base object. It holds a Counter, a Key Identifier Mode, a Security Level and an Algorithm. Algorithm 0 is CCM with AES-128 for encryption and message authentication, and RSA with SHA-256 for signatures. The levels cover a 4-byte or 8-byte message authentication code, with or without encryption, or a 2048-bit or 3072-bit signature. Receivers MUST drop messages that fail integrity checks. The Counter gives replay protection: each device remembers the last counter it has seen from each sender. Consistency Check messages let neighbors resynchronize counters and challenge each other with a nonce. The counter can also be a clock timestamp, which adds delay protection for devices with loosely synchronized clocks.

The Security Considerations section states that RPL networks face the same passive eavesdropping and active tampering as any other network, made harder by cheap devices that may lack a trusted computing base or a good random number generator, and by short-term trust relationships with devices that may never have communicated before. A group key used between peers protects only against outsiders: a malicious device inside the key-sharing group is not stopped. Public-key signatures, where used, give finer-grained origin authentication and evidence of who sent a message.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking messages is optional because many devices cannot pay the energy cost. When it is used, each message carries a counter so old messages cannot be replayed, and an authentication code that proves who sent it.

sections.title: Constants, Defaults and Registries
sections.content:
The RFC fixes a short list of constants. ROOT_RANK is the Rank of a DODAG root and equals MinHopRankIncrease, so its DAGRank is 1. BASE_RANK is 0, used by a virtual root that coordinates several physical roots. INFINITE_RANK is 0xFFFF, and RPL_DEFAULT_INSTANCE is 0. The default MinHopRankIncrease is 256, which gives Rank an 8-bit integer part. Default Trickle values are a DIO minimum interval exponent of 3 (an Imin of 8 ms), 20 doublings (a maximum interval of 2.3 hours) and a redundancy constant of 10; a redundancy constant of 0 means infinite, so a node never suppresses its DIOs. The default DAO delay is 1 second, and the default Path Control Size of 0 limits a node to sending a DAO to one parent.

Sequence counters for the DODAGVersionNumber, the DAOSequence and the Path Sequence use a 'lollipop' scheme: values from 128 up form a linear region used to bootstrap after a restart, and values up to 127 form a circular space of size 128. A comparison window of 16 (SEQUENCE_WINDOW) decides whether two values are comparable, and the recommended initial value is 240.

IANA created registries for the RPL control codes, the Mode of Operation, the control message options, Objective Code Points (none defined here), the security algorithm, security levels and the flags of each message and option. It allocated ICMPv6 Type 155, the ICMPv6 Destination Unreachable code 7 for 'Error in Source Routing Header', and the multicast address ff02::1a. This RFC defines the framework: the Objective Functions such as OF0 of RFC 6552, the metrics of RFC 6551, the data-plane option of RFC 6553 and the source-routing header of RFC 6554 are specified in companion documents.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC fixes a short list of default numbers, such as how often nodes advertise and how much rank each hop adds. Implementations may change them, but the defaults let devices work together out of the box.

items.title: O (Down)
items.text: Set when the packet is expected to progress Down; cleared when going toward the root.

items.title: R (Rank-Error)
items.text: Set on the first detected mismatch between Rank and direction; a second one means drop.

items.title: F (Forwarding-Error)
items.text: Set when a node cannot forward further, to clean up stale Downward state.

items.title: RPLInstanceID
items.text: Which Instance's DODAG the packet is using.

items.title: SenderRank
items.text: 16-bit field: zero from the source, DAGRank(rank) from a forwarding router.
